{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=responsibility+artificial+agency+accountability+decision+consequences&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"title\": [\"Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and societal decision processes, failures increasingly arise not from technical malfunction but from unresolved boundaries of authority, exception response, and accountability. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. On ETR, intentional actions are both the given attitudes and the exercises of our instrumental, rational powers.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198851486.003.0001\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2020, 11, 5]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/oso/9780198851486.003.0005\", \"title\": [\"Future-Directed Intentions and the Theory of Instrumental Rationality\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n               <jats:p>This chapter considers a major alternative to the extended theory of instrumental rationality (ETR): the view, pioneered by Michael Bratman, that future-directed intentions (FDIs) have a fundamental role to play in our understanding of the rationality of extended agency. The New Sociology of Science as the Foundation of the Epistemic Process: A Coherence–Persistence Rereading of Auguste Comte
Authors/Creators
Kriger, Boris
Description
The canonical reading of Auguste Comte places sociology at the apex of a hierarchical classification of the sciences, understood as the terminal discipline because it is the most complex and the most dependent on its predecessors. This paper argues that the canonical reading misidentifies the structural role sociology plays in Comte’s system. A careful rereading, combined with a formal framework developed in recent work on coherence and structural persistence, supports an alternative thesis: sociology is not the apex of the epistemic ladder but its
foundation
—the instance that determines, for any given community, which claims will be treated as real and which will be ignored and erased. Correctness plays only a secondary role in this determination; coherence plays a substantial one, and the coherence-persistence framework adopted here explains both facts. Knowledge without social persistence is not knowledge in any scientifically tractable sense; it is a private cognitive state structurally indistinguishable, at the level of collective inquiry, from the absence of that state. We formalize this intuition by modeling scientific knowledge as a persistent structure across a composite system comprising the individual, the stabilizing artifacts, the community, and the transmission channels, and by proving a Social Indistinguishability Theorem: in the absence of social persistence, the likelihood ratio between “the agent knows
” and “the agent does not know
” converges to unity for any external epistemic observer. A corollary gives the paper its slogan:
a thrice-Einstein without community is indistinguishable from a non-Einstein
. The result is then used to diagnose several open problems in contemporary philosophy of science and philosophy of mind, including the stalemate in scientific realism, the structural prospects of artificial agents as epistemic carriers, and the ongoing dispute concerning the scientific status of the concept of consciousness.
